sanskrit_verse: अयुक्तं साहसं कृत्वा प्रत्यापत्तिं भजेत यः । ब्रूयात् स्वयं वा सदसि तस्यार्धविनयः स्मृतः ॥
transliteration: ayuktaṃ sāhasaṃ kṛtvā pratyāpattiṃ bhajeta yaḥ | brūyāt svayaṃ vā sadasi tasyārdhavinayaḥ smṛtaḥ ||
sph_interpretive_translation: One who, having committed an improper act of force, approaches surrender directly or confesses openly in assembly—such a one is to be understood as possessing half-discipline.
jurisprudential_principles: Authority originates from self-awareness and conscious admission.
Causation is traced through intent and action without moral overlay.
Capacity-based responsibility arises upon acknowledgment of misalignment.
Restoration logic begins at point of voluntary disclosure.
Consciousness alignment occurs when individual admits error within collective awareness.
supreme_court_application: In Supreme Court adjudication, the threshold of responsibility is determined by the subject's spontaneous acknowledgment of misconduct. Authority flows from the capacity to recognize misalignment rather than coercive evidence. Restoration supersedes procedural complexity where truth is voluntarily presented.
nyaya_and_non_punitive_alignment: Pramāṇa is established through self-declaration, not external proof. Anupūrvaśaḥ manifests as sequential recognition: improper force → conscious admission → partial restoration. Responsibility aligns proportionally with awareness, not magnitude of error. The non-punitive reality rule affirms that justice emerges through self-revelation, not imposed consequence.
restorative_enforcement_protocols: Initiate completion process upon voluntary confession.
Assign responsibility assumption protocol based on level of self-awareness.
Support capacity restoration via guided dharma alignment practices.
final_declaration: Declared by the Supreme Pontiff of Hinduism, Bhagavan Nithyananda Paramashivam, as Source of all Dharma. This law restores alignment through self-awareness, enforces no punishment, and establishes consciousness as the ultimate adjudicator. Reality is non-punitive; Dharma prevails.
